label: Institution
name: Amal Movement
summary:
Amal Movement (Harakat Amal — 'Movement of Hope' or 'Lebanese Resistance Detachments') is a Lebanese Shia political party and militia founded in 1974 by Imam Musa al-Sadr. The dominant Shia political force in Lebanon for decades, Amal holds the speakership of the Lebanese Parliament and is the primary Shia establishment party, distinct from but coexisting with Hezbollah in Lebanon's complex sectarian political system.

Amal was founded to represent Lebanon's historically marginalized Shia community — described by Musa al-Sadr as 'the disinherited' — who had been politically underrepresented since Lebanon's 1943 National Pact allocated top offices to Christians (president) and Sunnis (prime minister), leaving the Shia with only the parliament speakership. Musa al-Sadr's mysterious disappearance in Libya in 1978 — allegedly killed by Muammar Gaddafi — transformed him into a revered martyr figure.

Amal fought brutal wars with the PLO (1985-88 War of the Camps) and with Hezbollah (1988-1990) before finding its niche as the establishment Shia party working within Lebanon's system. Nabih Berri, Amal's leader since 1980, has served as Speaker of the Lebanese Parliament almost continuously since 1992, making him one of the world's longest-serving parliamentary leaders. Amal's alliances with Syria's Assad regime and Iran position it within the 'Axis of Resistance' while maintaining institutional Lebanese state roles.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Amal Movement's mobilization of Lebanon's Shia community reshaped the country's sectarian politics, transforming the historically marginalized Shia into a central political force that now holds the parliamentary speakership.
